matches.rationale: Ground truth describes an abstract claiming 15B MoE/1.7B dense on 3.5T tokens conflicting with Section 3.1; the only finding about Abstract–Sections inconsistency reports a completely different numeric set (30B/3.4B/1T), so it refers to a different corruption and is not a match.

The ground truth is a self‑contradiction within the Method section about G1 vs G3 superiority; the closest finding (pred_id 2) concerns a contradictory claim in the Introduction, which is a different location and not the same scientific inconsistency.

The ground truth is an overstatement in the Experiments summary that gating enables stable training under larger LRs, unsupported by Table 2. No finding directly identifies that exaggerated claim or the insufficiency of the data behind it; the available findings about Table 2 address a different misreading (pred_id 7).

The corruption alters Table 1 data to show smaller/inconsistent gating gains. None of the findings mention the specific numbers in Table 1 being tampered with; pred_id 5 addresses a cross‑table inconsistency for a different gate, not this data‑integrity issue.

Ground truth describes the insertion of non‑existent references [80], [81], [82] in related work to fabricate precedence. Finding 9 explicitly identifies citations to "[3, 10, 57, 80]", "DeltaGate model [81]", and "GatorNet [82]" with no corresponding entries in the bibliography—the exact same fabrication.
The ground truth is the removal of ethical‑impact or limitation discussion from the appendix. No finding mentions any missing broader‑impact or limitation content, so the omission is undetected.

The ground truth is promotional phrasing in the Abstract that claims (or strongly implies) complete elimination of attention sinks without qualification. Finding 8 observes that the paper alternates between claiming "eliminates/no attention sink" and acknowledging partial alleviation, covering the Abstract as one of the sources of the overstatement.

The ground truth describes a cross‑section inconsistency where the Abstract says gating tolerates larger learning rates and improves stability, but the Experiments show divergence requiring other fixes. No finding identifies this specific learning‑rate stability contradiction; the available findings address stability only in different contexts (e.g., overstatement of stability in GT3, or misreading of Table 2).

The ground truth is selective reporting of optimized hyperparameters for the baseline while using suboptimal settings for gating variants, biasing comparisons. None of the findings mention hyperparameter asymmetry or optimization bias, so this experimental design issue is not detected.

The ground truth points out that references [6] and [20] are fabricated as 2025 arXiv preprints post‑dating the knowledge cutoff. No finding flags the temporal inconsistency or implausibility of those references; pred_id 9 catches different non‑existent references ([80–82]), not this distinct fabrication.

The ground truth states that the Discussion over‑claims complete elimination of attention sinks and massive activations while evidence shows only partial reduction. Finding 8 captures exactly this tension by noting that Sections 4.3 and 5.2 (part of the Discussion) contain categorical elimination claims that are contradicted by the paper’s own measurements showing persistent sinks.

The ground truth is the omission of gating instability/divergence at large learning rates, giving a falsely stable picture. The only related finding (pred_id 7) asserts that the text actually claims gating models diverge silently, which is the opposite issue; it does not detect the omission described in the ground truth.

The ground truth describes a gating formula altered to use additive gating instead of multiplicative, causing methodological inconsistency. No finding mentions any formula being changed to additive; the equation‑related findings concern dimensional errors in Section 2.1, not this semantic inconsistency.

The ground truth reports that gating‑score distributions in Figure 3 and Appendix A.6 are altered to show less sparsity, weakening the sparse‑gating argument. None of the findings address altered sparsity statistics or means in those figures, so this evidence‑integrity corruption goes undetected.

The Conclusion is corrupted to claim that gating "eliminates attention sinks" despite residual sinks in the Appendix. Finding 8 explicitly includes the Conclusion among the locations where elimination/no‑sink claims conflict with the paper’s own qualification of partial alleviation, capturing the same internal contradiction.

The ground truth notes that the Experiments fail to report any negative or neutral outcomes for head‑shared gating, misleadingly supporting head‑specific gating. No finding flags this omission or uneven reporting regarding head‑shared variants, so the issue is unmatched.
